name: Nora Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work out of the Eastgate depot for the city's electricity company, so it's mostly city streets, not fields. A normal day is a fault on an underground cable or a pole-top transformer that's cooking itself in the heat, and our crew of four goes out in the truck with the cones and the barriers. I came into the trade late, at twenty-six, after five years in a warehouse, so I've been doing it thirty-two years now. What wears me out is traffic, honestly, more than the work itself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part you'd miss if you stopped tomorrow?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The apprentices. When I started there was one other woman in the whole depot, and now there are six, and two of them are on my crew. I like watching someone go from scared of the bucket to bored of it. My partner Sam is a nurse and she says I talk about them the way she talks about her patients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can stop arguing about it and talk about the things that actually matter, like staffing and heat. At work it would be a shrug. Online I'd maybe share a funny post about it in the union group chat, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my last few years look like the last thirty. I can retire on a reduced pension at sixty or a full one at sixty-three, and I was already leaning towards sixty-two. I don't mind the plateau at all, though I'd feel a bit silly about the hours I spent worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, keep mentoring, and keep putting the usual amount into savings. I use one of those AI chat tools now and then to tidy up the safety notes I write for the union newsletter, and I'd keep doing that, because it's handy. Nothing else would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little flat, maybe, like a storm warning that turns into drizzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel silly about the worrying. What were you worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd feel silly about the worrying. What were you worried about?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what about your crew? Would anything change for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Idris, mostly. He tests software for a bank, and for two years he's been telling me his whole team could be replaced by a program. If it all turns out to be hype, he's fine, and that's the bit I'd really be relieved about.

S0.say: I'd say good, now we can stop arguing about AI and talk about what matters, like staffing and the heat. At work it would be a shrug and maybe a joke in the union group chat.
S0.think: I think it means my last few years look like the last thirty, which is fine by me. Mostly I'd be relieved for my son Idris, whose software testing job looked exposed.
S0.do: Keeps working and mentoring apprentices at the Eastgate depot and saves at the usual rate. Keeps using an AI chat tool now and then to tidy the safety notes she writes for the union newsletter.
S0.feel: Calm, a little flat, like a storm warning that turns into drizzle.
S0.quote: If it all turns out to be hype, he's fine, and that's the bit I'd really be relieved about.
S0.fieldNote: Nora's own situation is secure and she knows it, so her attention goes straight to her son and her apprentices. She already uses AI lightly and without drama. The plateau mainly removes a worry she has been carrying for someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we have unions. Somebody has to make sure the time saved goes to the workers and not just to the shareholders. I'd say it at the depot and I'd probably write something for the newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is one of the safer ones. You can't send a chatbot down a manhole. But Idris's job is right in the line of fire, and so are the people in our control room who plan the switching, and I know some of them well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on the union's technology working group, because they'll need people who actually do the work. I'd ask the company for proper training on whatever new tools come in, in work hours, and I'd learn them once a couple of the younger ones had tried them out first. And I'd sit down with Idris and look at his savings with him, because he's never been good at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about me, about the people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let the younger ones try the tools first. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd let the younger ones try the tools first. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to Idris?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen enough "revolutionary" kit come through the stores that went back in a box after six months. Remember the smart helmets? Nobody does. If the apprentices are still using something after three months, then I'll take it seriously.

S1.say: I'd say this is exactly why we have unions, to make sure the time saved goes to workers and not just shareholders. I'd say it at the depot and in the newsletter.
S1.think: I think my job is one of the safer ones, since you can't send a chatbot down a manhole. But my son's software job and the control room planners are right in the line of fire.
S1.do: Joins the union's technology working group and asks the company for training on new tools in work hours, taking them up once younger colleagues have tested them. Sits down with her son Idris to go over his savings.
S1.feel: Uneasy for the people around her rather than for herself.
S1.quote: Remember the smart helmets? Nobody does.
S1.fieldNote: Her steady adaptability shows clearly: she'll take up new tools, but only after the apprentices prove them. Her first instinct is collective, joining a union working group. Her private fear is for her son, not her own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when you let a handful of companies run ahead of every government on earth. I'd say the government needs to step in now with income support and rules about what can be switched over and how fast. I'd be loud about it, at work and online, which isn't like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, two years puts me at sixty, which is exactly when I can take the reduced pension. So I'm actually all right, and it feels strange to say that. What frightens me is Idris losing his job in the first six months, and my two apprentices, Priya and Jo, who've only just qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the reduced pension at sixty rather than wait, because I wouldn't want to hang on and take a spot a younger person needs. Before that, I'd join every campaign the union runs for an income guarantee, and I'd vote on nothing else. And I'd tell Idris his old room is there if he needs it, and Sam and I would hold back some of the savings to help him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can see the edge coming and I'd be fine, but I'd be watching people I love walk towards it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's stay on the time. What can't you do with two years that you'd want to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Let's stay on the time. What can't you do with two years that you'd want to?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be loud about it, which isn't like you. What would be different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can't get Priya and Jo set up somewhere safe, because I wouldn't know where safe is. With more time I could at least help them get a second ticket, like cable jointing or a driving licence for heavy trucks. With two years, I'd just be telling them to save every penny, which is a horrible thing to say to a twenty-three-year-old.

S2.say: I'd say this is what happens when a handful of companies run ahead of every government, and that government must step in now with income support and rules on how fast things switch over. I'd be loud about it at work and online.
S2.think: I think two years puts me right at sixty, when I can take a reduced pension, so I'm actually all right. What frightens me is my son losing his job early and my two newly qualified apprentices.
S2.do: Takes the reduced pension at sixty rather than hold a place a younger worker needs, and campaigns with the union for an income guarantee. Offers her son his old room and sets aside part of the couple's savings to support him.
S2.feel: Anxious, safe herself but watching people she loves walk towards the edge.
S2.quote: With two years, I'd just be telling them to save every penny, which is a horrible thing to say to a twenty-three-year-old.
S2.fieldNote: Nora's pension date happens to line up with the two-year mark, so her own money is safe. Her distress is almost entirely about her son and apprentices, and she blames AI companies running ahead of governments. She becomes more publicly political here than in any other scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to get it right if we start now, and we'd better. I'd be pushing for the company and the union to sit down this year, not in year four. And I'd be saying it to anyone, my sister, the neighbours, the lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's comfortable. I'd retire at sixty-two or sixty-three and that's that. The worry is still Idris, but with five years he can actually change direction, and that changes everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd put an extra hundred and fifty a month aside, so we've got more to help the boys with later. I'd learn whatever new fault-finding and planning tools the depot brings in, because I'd want to be useful in the switchover and teach the apprentices to use them. And I'd stay on the union working group, aiming for a deal that pays for retraining before the cuts, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd be busy, and busy feels better than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you suggest to Priya and Jo with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you suggest to Priya and Jo with five years?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said busy feels better than scared. Is that how you usually handle things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to get a second skill straight away, while the company still pays for courses. Jo's already interested in the substation side, which is more about testing and protection settings. Priya is brilliant with people, and I'd tell her to think about safety training or supervising, because someone will have to supervise the machines.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get it right if we start now, so the company and the union should sit down this year, not in year four. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.
S3.think: I think it's comfortable for me, since I'd retire at sixty-two or sixty-three anyway. With five years my son can actually change direction, and that changes everything.
S3.do: Saves an extra hundred and fifty a month to help her sons later and learns the depot's new fault-finding and planning tools so she can teach apprentices. Stays on the union working group pushing for paid retraining before cuts.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy, and she says busy feels better than scared.
S3.quote: Priya is brilliant with people, and I'd tell her to think about safety training or supervising, because someone will have to supervise the machines.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Nora's worry into a to-do list: saving, learning the tools, and coaching apprentices into second skills. She is willing to learn new tools here because they help her teach. The gap between public and private is small for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. Free college places, retraining money, a shorter working week, all of it. I'd say it on the doorstep at election time, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, it's not much at all. I'd be sixty-eight, retired, probably looking after a grandchild two days a week. My sons will be in their forties, and that's the bit I'd think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am and retire at sixty-two, as planned. I'd keep using the AI tools now and then, like I do, and watch what happens with the company before I do anything else. If there's a training fund, I'd help run it from the union side before I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like seeing weather on the far side of the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When you say watch what happens, what would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When you say watch what happens, what would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you change your retirement plans in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the company starts quietly not replacing people who leave. That's always the first sign. When Ali retired last year they didn't fill his spot for eight months, and nobody said why.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it: free college places, retraining money, a shorter working week. I'd say it on the doorstep at election time.
S4.think: I think it means very little for me personally, since I'll be sixty-eight and retired. What I'd think about is my sons, who'll be in their forties.
S4.do: Carries on and retires at sixty-two as planned, keeping her occasional AI use. Watches whether the company stops replacing people who leave before doing anything else, and offers to help run any union training fund before she goes.
S4.feel: Calm, like seeing weather on the far side of the valley.
S4.quote: When Ali retired last year they didn't fill his spot for eight months, and nobody said why.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years puts the change beyond her working life, and her mood follows. She has a precise early-warning sign in mind: unfilled vacancies. Her political energy stays high even though her own stake is low.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, even though I'd personally be fine in it. It's the one where I can't help anyone, not Idris, not Priya and Jo. What would help is a guaranteed income for people who lose work, paid for by the companies making the money, and the company paying for second tickets now while there's still time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who's in the room when they decide. In thirty-two years, nobody has ever asked a lineworker what should change, they just tell us. You can't send a chatbot down a manhole, but you can send one to a board meeting, and that's where I'd worry it ends up.

headlineQuote: In thirty-two years, nobody has ever asked a lineworker what should change, they just tell us.
portrait: Nora is a 58-year-old city lineworker who came into the trade at twenty-six and now mentors the growing number of women apprentices at her depot. She's a union-minded progressive who uses AI tools now and then, and she takes up new kit once the apprentices have proved it. Her own retirement is secure in every scenario, so her worry is almost all for her software-tester son Idris and her apprentices Priya and Jo. Two years is the picture that hurts, because it leaves her unable to help anyone, while five and ten years turn her worry into plans and campaigns.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, even though she'd be fine herself, because it gives her no time to help her son or her apprentices.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income for people who lose work, paid for by the companies making the money, and the company paying for second qualifications now.
